readingNote: The radical name is gǔn. Shù names the vertical stroke shape; it is not the selected radical reading.
The radical reading is zhǔ. Diǎn is the everyday name of a dot stroke.

shape: 人 spreads across a full square, while 亻 narrows into a left-side column. In 你 and 他, leave the larger right component enough room instead of shrinking the whole character.
usage: This family often concerns people, roles, or human activity. The radical does not tell you which person a pronoun refers to; the rest of the character and the word still matter.
practice: Compare the pronouns 你 and 他, then add 们 to form 你们 and 他们. Print the three example characters and keep the left column equally narrow.

readingNote: Rén is the traditional radical-table reading. Do not confuse this heading with simplified 儿 (ér), corresponding to 兒 in words such as 儿子.
Kǎn is used in the cited radical tables; qiǎn is also recorded in other dictionary traditions.

shape: 刀 has a bent hook and a falling stroke as a whole character. At the right of 刻 it becomes 刂, two vertical strokes with a hook on the longer one.
usage: Cutting is a helpful clue in 切, but 分 can refer to minutes or scores. In 切, the qiē reading belongs to cutting; qiè occurs in words such as 一切.
practice: Print 分, 切, and 刻. Circle the knife form in each and compare its position before following the whole character's stroke sequence.

shape: 力 contains a turning hook crossed by a left-falling stroke. It may sit at the right, as in 功, or to the left of another component, as in 加.
usage: Effort and force help connect some members of this family, but adding in 加 is not a literal picture of strength. Dictionary grouping is a lookup aid, not a complete definition.
practice: Write 功 and 动 in adjoining rows to compare right-side 力, then move to 加 and leave room for 口 on the right.

readingNote: Bǔ is the divination reading. Neutral bo occurs in words such as 萝卜 and is not the radical heading used here.
This historical cliff radical is hǎn. Simplified 厂 meaning factory, corresponding to 廠, is chǎng.

shape: 口 is a small box made with three strokes, not four separate sides. Its width and height shrink when it stands beside a larger right-hand component.
usage: Eating, drinking, and calling give three direct mouth-related examples. Other 口 characters are sound transcriptions or particles, so do not assume every member describes a mouth action.
practice: Say 吃, 喝, and 叫 before writing them. Keep 口 consistent across all three rows while changing the right component.

shape: 囗 surrounds the contents of a character and is larger than the separate mouth radical 口. Write the inside before closing the enclosure's bottom line.
usage: 国 and 园 suggest bounded spaces, whereas 回 has developed the meaning return. The enclosure distinguishes this dictionary family from characters with a small mouth component.
practice: Print 国, 回, and 园. Check that the inner components have breathing room and that the outer bottom is written after the contents.

shape: 土 has a vertical crossing two horizontals, with the lower horizontal longer as a standalone form. On the left, that lower stroke is often written as a rising stroke.
usage: Ground and built places connect 地 and 城. 坏 shows why a radical clue cannot replace learning a word's modern meaning. 地 is dì for ground, but de as a grammatical particle.
practice: Practise 地, 坏, and 城 side by side. Keep the earth component narrow and identify which example has a meaning that is no longer transparently earth-related.

readingNote: Xī is used in mainland Mandarin and this directory. Taiwan references may use xì for the evening character.

shape: 女 changes proportion on the left of 好, 妈, and 姐. Its crossing strokes must fit inside a narrow column while the right component occupies the rest of the square.
usage: Kinship words make the family easy to recognise, but historical character categories are not rules about modern gender roles. 好 means good and should be learned as a complete word.
practice: Use 妈妈 and 姐姐 to recall the family words, then write 好. Compare the compressed left 女 with standalone 女 before printing another row.

shape: 子 has a curved hook, a crossing horizontal, and an upper turning stroke. Its lower horizontal may rise when the component sits on the left, as in 孩 and 孙.
usage: Child-related meanings are visible in 孩 and 孙. 字 means a written character, so grouping it under 子 does not make its modern meaning child.
practice: Compare 子 at the bottom of 字 with its left-side form in 孩 and 孙. Print the three examples and mark the change in the crossing stroke.
readingNote: Use full third-tone zǐ for the radical. Neutral zi occurs as a suffix in words such as 本子.

shape: 宀 is a three-stroke roof: a top dot, a short left dot, and a horizontal hook. It must shelter the lower components without flattening them.
usage: Homes and rooms give a useful connection for 家 and 室. 安 has a historical construction, but its modern meaning should not be reduced to a literal claim about the components underneath a roof.
practice: Place 家, 安, and 室 on one worksheet. Align the roof heights, then compare how much vertical space each lower part needs.
readingNote: Mián is the selected radical reading; 宝盖头 (bǎogàitóu) is a descriptive classroom name, not the isolated reading gài.
Wāng is the radical-table reading. Other readings, including yóu, occur in dictionaries for the independent character.

shape: 山 has one tall middle vertical and shorter sides. In 岩 it sits at the top; in 峰 it is compressed on the left rather than stretched across the square.
usage: Mountain and landscape meanings connect these examples. A similar silhouette is not enough for dictionary classification: 出 is not assigned to the 山 radical here.
practice: Write standalone 山 first, then compare its top position in 岩 with its narrow left position in 峰. Keep the middle stroke tallest in each form.

readingNote: Use gān here. The gàn reading belongs to other uses of simplified 干, including forms corresponding to 幹.
The historical shelter radical is yǎn. Simplified 广 for 廣, meaning broad, is guǎng; some reference tables use a different tone for the radical name.

shape: 心 often sits beneath a character, as in 想 and 忘. On the left it becomes 忄, with two dots around a vertical; those side strokes are not copied from the full bottom form.
usage: Thought, memory, and feelings often belong here. 忙 means busy, and its heart component offers a broad mental-state clue rather than a literal anatomical definition.
practice: Print 想, 忘, and 忙. Separate bottom-form practice from left-form practice, then check the dots against each character's animation.

shape: 手 becomes 扌 at the left: a short horizontal, a vertical hook, and a rising stroke. Keep this three-stroke form distinct from the fuller standalone 手.
usage: Physical action is clear in 打 and 提, but 找 means look for and cannot be decoded by a hand picture alone. 提 also has other readings in particular words; tí is the lift or mention reading here.
practice: Make a worksheet with 打, 找, and 提. Keep the same left-column width in every row, then say a useful action phrase for each.

readingNote: Dǒu names the dipper or measure. Dòu meaning fight corresponds to traditional 鬥, a different Kangxi radical.

shape: 日 encloses one interior horizontal. In these examples it stands on the left, so the box is narrower than a standalone 日 and must leave room for the right component.
usage: Brightness connects 明 to the sun; time words connect 时 and 昨 to days and moments. 明天 and 昨天 are useful opposites, not interchangeable readings of the same character.
practice: Print 明, 时, and 昨 together. Practise a narrow 日 first, then add each distinct right-hand shape while keeping the boxes level.

shape: 月 is a narrow form with two short inner horizontals. 朋 repeats it side by side, while 服 places a different component on the right.
usage: The visible 月 form can also represent the meat radical in body-part characters. Do not classify every moon-shaped component as radical 74; this set follows the stated dictionary data.
practice: Compare 月 and 朋 before writing 服. Use the lookup on a body-part character such as 肚 to see why shape and dictionary radical are separate questions.

shape: 木 has a central vertical crossed by a horizontal and two spreading strokes. On the left of 校, the right-falling stroke is shortened so it does not collide with 交.
usage: Trees are clear in 林, while 本 adds a mark near the root. 校 commonly means school and is xiào in 学校; jiào is a different reading in words about checking or comparing.
practice: Print 本, 林, and 校. Compare the added line in 本, repeated trees in 林, and compressed left tree in 校 before practising from memory.

shape: 水 often changes to the three-stroke left form 氵. The strokes are individually shaped and spaced; the lowest one rises toward the right component.
usage: River, sea, and washing give direct water connections. The radical alone cannot predict pronunciation: 河, 海, and 洗 have different initials and tones.
practice: Use 河, 海, and 洗 as a short water worksheet. Keep 氵 equally narrow and compare the right components rather than repeating three identical dots.

shape: 火 stands on the left of 灯 and 烧. At the bottom of 热 it appears as four separate dots, 灬, spread beneath the upper structure.
usage: Light and heat connect these examples, but not every occurrence of four bottom dots has an obvious modern fire meaning. Check the whole character before making a semantic claim.
practice: Compare 灯 and 烧 first, then write 热 with four distinct bottom dots. Keep those dots low enough to support the upper strokes.

readingNote: Qiáng is used by the cited traditional radical tables; pán is the common mainland reading of this character.

shape: 犬 becomes 犭 on the left: a slant, a curved hook, and another slant. It is not the two-stroke person form 亻.
usage: This animal family includes more than dogs: 猫 is a cat and 狼 is a wolf. The radical supplies a broad animal association, while the whole word names the species.
practice: Print 狗, 猫, and 狼 in adjacent rows. Trace 犭 carefully before adding each right part, and contrast it with 亻 in 你.

shape: The jade component usually appears as 王 on the left of these characters. Its final horizontal is compressed into a rising stroke; the standalone 玉 has an additional dot.
usage: Objects and qualities historically associated with jade extend into modern words such as 玩 and 理. The common left form looks like 王, but its radical family is 玉.
practice: Compare 玉 and 王 first, then write 玩, 理, and 球. Notice that the left-side form does not keep the standalone jade dot.

shape: 田 is a box divided by a vertical and a horizontal. It can sit at the top, as in 男 and 界, or at the left, as in 畔.
usage: Field and boundary associations are more transparent in 畔 and 界 than in 男. Treat these as historical dictionary groupings, not rules for translating every character.
practice: Use 男, 界, and 畔 to practise moving 田 from the top to the left. Keep all four inner spaces open and reasonably balanced.

readingNote: Shū is the foot and radical reading. Pǐ is a separate cloth-measure sense, not the meaning selected here.
Nè is a dictionary reading of this sickness radical; chuáng and other readings appear in traditional radical-name references.

shape: 目 is a tall box with two inner horizontals. It stands on the left in 眼 and 睛, but beneath the upper strokes in 看.
usage: Seeing and eyes connect this family directly. 看 is kàn for looking or reading, while kān is used for looking after or guarding in other words.
practice: Print 眼, 睛, and 看. Compare the two interior lines of 目 with the single line inside 日 before writing the complete characters.

shape: 石 has an upper horizontal and falling stroke above a small 口. At the left, keep the lower box tucked below the upper stroke rather than stretched wide.
usage: Hard material connects 石 and 硬, but 码 often means code or a unit and is not literally stone. 破 can describe breaking many kinds of objects.
practice: Write 码, 破, and 硬 with a consistent narrow 石. Say the full word 电话号码 for 码 so the practice connects shape to a real use.

shape: 禾 resembles 木 with an additional short upper slant. When it is a left component, shorten the right-falling stroke to leave space beside it.
usage: Crops and seasons connect 禾 with 秋 and 种. 科 has extended uses such as a school subject. 种 is zhǒng for a seed or kind, but zhòng for planting.
practice: Print 秋, 种, and 科. Check the short slant that distinguishes 禾 from 木, then practise the two readings of 种 in separate words.

shape: 竹 becomes a compact six-stroke top form, ⺮, above each example. Its two groups need equal height but should not be squeezed into one solid horizontal bar.
usage: Writing tools connect naturally to bamboo in 笔. 笑 and 等 show that a radical may preserve historical grouping without explaining a modern everyday meaning.
practice: Print 笔, 笑, and 等. Leave room under ⺮ for three different lower structures and keep the six top strokes separated.

shape: 米 places two short upper strokes around a central 木-like framework. At the left of a character, narrow its spreading lower strokes.
usage: Powder, grains, and refining form a useful material-related group. 精 also appears in abstract words, so its meaning cannot be reduced to rice alone.
practice: Write 粉, 粒, and 精. Keep the central line clear and compare the lower right stroke of left-side 米 with standalone 米.

shape: Traditional left-side 糹 becomes simplified 纟. The examples here use the simplified three-stroke form; the historical head radical 糸 has six strokes.
usage: Thread and textile associations underlie many members, but colours and paper are learned as full words. A simplified character's radical shape need not have the same stroke count as its Kangxi heading.
practice: Print 红, 绿, and 纸. Practise the three-stroke 纟 separately and compare it with 糸 in the reference grid without mixing their sequences.

readingNote: Gèn is the radical and stopping reading; gěn occurs in other descriptive uses.

shape: The historical six-stroke heading 艸 commonly appears as 艹 on top. Regional writing standards can count or shape this top form differently; follow the displayed character animation.
usage: Flowers, grass, and tea provide clear plant-related examples. The six-stroke classification of 艸 is not a claim that every modern 艹 top uses six strokes.
practice: Print 花, 草, and 茶, then compare the lower shapes under the shared top. Keep the grass component wide enough to cover each body.

readingNote: Chóng is the familiar insect reading. Huǐ is the older snake-related reading retained in some radical tables.

shape: 言 becomes 訁 as a traditional left component and 讠 in simplified writing. These examples use 讠, whose dot is separate from the lower turning stroke.
usage: Speaking, speech, and language give direct clues in 说, 话, and 语. 说 has other readings in certain words; shuō is the ordinary speak reading used here.
practice: Build a worksheet with 说, 话, and 语. Keep 讠 narrow and name a spoken-language phrase before writing each row.

shape: 辵 is the historical heading; 辶 is the common surrounding form. In these examples, write the inner component before the long lower sweep of 辶.
usage: Movement is visible in 进, while 近 means near and 这 means this. A walking radical does not turn every member into a motion verb.
practice: Practise 进 and 近 together, noting 井 versus 斤 inside, then add 这. Let the final sweep support the inside instead of cutting across it.

shape: The full 金 heading has eight strokes. Traditional left-side 釒 simplifies to the five-stroke 钅 seen in these examples.
usage: Iron and silver are metals, and money historically connects to metal coins. The modern use of 钱 includes money that is not physically made of metal.
practice: Print 钱, 铁, and 银. Learn the left-side 钅 sequence once, then compare the distinct right components and spoken tones.

readingNote: Cháng matches long and the radical heading. Zhǎng means grow or senior in other words.
Lì is used in modern simplified 隶 corresponding to 隸. Traditional radical tables also call this heading dài; do not treat slave as a complete definition of every indexed character.

This radical groups many head-related characters. Yè is its conventional radical name and the modern page reading; xié is recorded for the historical head sense. Leaf here would misleadingly suggest a plant leaf.
Lì names the ancient cooking vessel and this radical. Gé is a different reading in other historical uses.
Mǐn is the conventional radical-table reading. The old frog word also has the reading měng; miǎn is recorded in other traditions and contexts.
